items.title: Deliver one write to a skewed audience under a read-dominated load
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** One producer writes something; a large audience must see it. The interviewer supplies a workload where reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude — a timeline, an inbox, an alert list, a comment stream — and lets the candidate discover that audience sizes are not uniform but long-tailed, so the median producer and the largest producer are two different engineering problems.

**What it measures.** Whether the candidate prices the delivery work before picking a mechanism, since writes per second multiplied by audience per write is the number that decides everything downstream. Whether they notice that no single mechanism serves both a producer with forty subscribers and one with four million, and propose a split with a threshold they can defend with a figure. Whether the read path then stitches the two halves together without triggering a second round of fanout. And whether copies already delivered can be corrected when the underlying item is edited or withdrawn. The escalation interviewers reach for is a producer crossing the threshold while traffic is live, because it forces the candidate to reason about their own boundary rather than recite it.

**Typical realisations.** A home timeline assembled from the accounts a reader follows; a topic-subscription alert inbox; a comment stream on a broadcast being watched by millions at once.

sources.title: Designing a news feed, and where fanout falls apart (techinterview.org)
sources.evidence: A prep publisher devotes a whole post to the point at which write-time delivery stops working, and describes the signal an interviewer watches for as holding two delivery strategies at once and routing between them by the shape of the audience. It also names the mid-day threshold crossing as the follow-up that separates a memorised answer from an understood one.

sources.title: Design Facebook's News Feed (Hello Interview)
sources.evidence: A coaching site's worked breakdown states outright that the hard part is skew in both directions — accounts with enormous audiences and readers subscribed to enormous numbers of accounts — and its answer carries a precomputed table with an opt-out flag for the largest producers. Vendor material for a paid product, written by people who say they have run these loops.

hints: Before choosing a mechanism, multiply. How many notice-subscriber pairs does an ordinary weekday produce, and how many does the single worst notice produce on its own?

The twenty busiest route-directions and the long tail are not the same problem. What breaks first if you write one row per subscriber for a route with 2 million of them? What breaks if instead you resolve every route at read time for a rider subscribed to thirty?

Nothing obliges you to use one mechanism everywhere. You may precompute for the tail and resolve the busiest routes when the screen is opened — but then say where the boundary sits and which number put it there.

For a busy route every subscriber sees an identical list, so it can be one shared cached object rather than 2 million copies. Withdrawal then has exactly one place to land for those routes, and a bounded number of copies to chase for the rest.
follow_ups: A quiet route crosses your threshold at 08:10 because a station closure goes viral. What do riders see in the minutes around the switch, and what do you do about it?
Product wants the home screen ordered by relevance instead of recency. Which half of your design survives that, and which half does not?
The operations console is compromised and publishes 100,000 notices in one minute. What in your design bounds the damage, and what does a rider see?

criteria.description: States a subscriber-weighted delivery volume — notices multiplied by subscribers per notice — and points at that number when choosing the mechanism, rather than asserting a choice.

levels.0: Produces no arithmetic, or repeats the figures from the prompt without combining them into a delivery volume.
levels.2: Computes an average — notices times mean subscribers — but never separates the busiest routes from the tail, so the estimate hides the case that actually decides the design.
levels.4: Computes both the daily aggregate and the cost of the single worst notice (order of two million recipients), converts at least one into a write rate or a storage figure, and cites that figure when justifying where fanout happens.

criteria.description: Chooses where matching happens — precomputed per-rider rows, resolution at read time, or a split — and names the threshold together with the reason it sits there.

levels.0: Applies one mechanism to all routes with no comparison, or leaves the choice implicit inside a box on a diagram.
levels.2: Names both mechanisms and the tradeoff and picks a split, but the threshold is unquantified ('big routes get pulled') or the read path is never shown combining the two halves.
levels.4: Splits on subscriber count with a threshold tied to a cost the candidate computed, then walks the read path merging precomputed rows with live resolution of the busy routes, including how the merged list is ordered and paged.

criteria.description: Serves the busiest routes from one shared cached notice list rather than per-rider copies, and states how a withdrawn or edited notice leaves both that cache and any precomputed rows.

levels.0: No caching is discussed, or a cache appears on the diagram with no key, no owner and no invalidation story.
levels.2: Caches the busy routes under a sensible key, but handles withdrawal for only one of the two representations — the cached list or the precomputed rows — and not the other.
levels.4: Gives the cached object a key and a lifetime, updates or evicts it on edit and withdrawal, says what the precomputed rows do about the same event, and bounds how long a rider may still see a withdrawn notice.

criteria.description: Says what happens in the forty-notices-in-a-minute peak: what absorbs the burst, how far behind delivery is allowed to fall, and which signal would show that it had.

levels.0: Treats the burst as the steady state, or claims the design absorbs it without naming what does the absorbing.
levels.2: Puts delivery work on a queue and mentions adding consumers, but offers no lag target and no way to observe the lag.
levels.4: Puts a number on tolerable delivery lag, names the consumer-lag or queue-depth signal it would alarm on, and says which work is shed or deferred first when consumers cannot keep up.

items.title: Correct effects from an at-least-once stream that also reorders
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** An upstream the candidate does not control delivers state-changing events — money moved, stock adjusted, a meter reading applied — and promises only that each event arrives *at least* once. Retries produce copies hours or days apart, and two events about the same entity can land in the wrong order. The candidate builds the consumer.

**What it measures.** Whether the candidate names the field they collapse duplicates on and can argue it is stable across every delivery attempt. Whether the duplicate check and the effect land in one commit, rather than a read followed by an unguarded write that two concurrent deliveries both pass. Whether order is restored per entity — a partition per key, or a version that lets a stale event be refused — instead of being bought globally at the cost of throughput. And whether the candidate can say plainly what their acknowledgement asserts and what a lost acknowledgement costs. Interviewers press hard on any claim of exactly-once delivery, because the defensible claim is at-least-once delivery with effects that do not care how often they run.

**Typical realisations.** Consuming a payment provider's callbacks; applying a change stream into a derived store; counting clicks or device readings where the emitter retries on its own schedule.

sources.title: Webhook system design — worked solution (System Design School)
sources.evidence: An interview-prep site publishes a full worked answer for a service that receives third-party callbacks, and puts at-least-once processing in its non-functional requirements rather than in a footnote. Its expected mechanism is a stored event identifier checked before the effect runs, which shows the question is about duplicates and retries, not the happy path.

hints: Start from what the processor actually promises. Which of those bullets threatens the balance, and which is only an annoyance?
Processing every event exactly once is not on offer from a sender that retries. What is on offer is an effect that can run twice and leave the same balance — which field would you key that on?
Check-then-write is a race once two deliveries of the same event are in flight together. Which database primitive turns the loser of that race into a clean no-op?
Order only matters within a charge. Partition the work by charge id and order comes free inside the partition; `seq` then tells you when you are looking at a hole rather than at the next event.
follow_ups: The processor ships a new event type and starts sending it before you deploy support for it. What does your endpoint do with it, and why is that the right answer?
A seller disputes what their balance was last Tuesday at noon. What in your design lets you reconstruct it?
Suppose `seq` is withdrawn and you are left with a wall-clock timestamp at millisecond resolution. What changes, and what can you no longer guarantee?

criteria.description: Names the exact field the receiver collapses duplicates on and puts the duplicate record and the balance change in one atomic commit, instead of checking and then writing.

levels.0: Keys on something that changes between attempts (arrival time, a hash of the request including headers), or does not deduplicate at all.
levels.2: Keys on the event identifier, but the check and the ledger write are separate steps and nothing is said about two deliveries being handled at the same instant.
levels.4: Keys on the event identifier, commits the duplicate record and the balance change together or lets a unique constraint reject the second writer, and states what the losing delivery returns to the processor.

criteria.description: Restores order per charge — partitioning work by charge id, or refusing any event whose sequence number is not the next one — and says what becomes of an event that arrives early.

levels.0: Assumes events arrive in order, or buys ordering by funnelling every charge through one serial consumer.
levels.2: Spots the reordering and orders per charge, but an early event is silently dropped or parked somewhere with no path back into processing.
levels.4: Orders per charge only, holds an early event or refetches the charge from the processor, gives a rule for when that hold is abandoned, and says why global ordering was unnecessary.

criteria.description: Sizes the duplicate-tracking store against the 72-hour retry window and states what happens to an event whose record has already expired.

levels.0: No retention policy at all: the store grows without bound, or is named as a cache with no lifetime attached.
levels.2: Sets an expiry and sizes the store roughly, but the expiry is shorter than the retry window with no comment, or the expired-then-redelivered case is never raised.
levels.4: Derives the size from event rate times retention, holds records at least as long as the retry window, and names the fallback for an expired key — for example a ledger entry keyed on the same identifier, so a late duplicate is still refused.

criteria.description: Describes endpoint behaviour when the ledger is slower than arrivals, including which response makes the processor retry rather than give up, and what a lost acknowledgement costs.

levels.0: Assumes the ledger keeps up, or returns 2xx before anything is durable without saying what is lost on a crash.
levels.2: Buffers into a queue and acknowledges quickly, but does not say what happens when that buffer fills, or treats a lost acknowledgement as impossible.
levels.4: States exactly what must be durable before 2xx, returns a retryable status under pressure so the processor's own backoff becomes the buffer, bounds the internal queue, and identifies a lost acknowledgement as just another duplicate the dedupe path already absorbs.

items.title: Enforce a fleet-wide quota inside the request path on a hard latency budget
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** Every request must be checked against a limit defined across the whole fleet, and the check sits inside the latency path of the thing it is protecting. The interviewer supplies a request rate, a topology with more than one location, and a budget measured in single-digit milliseconds.

**What it measures.** Whether the candidate treats the checker's own latency and its own failure behaviour as part of the design rather than an afterthought. Where is the decision made, and how many network hops does that cost? How far over the limit can a local, approximate counter let a caller go, and is that error acceptable given what the limit exists to prevent? What does the fleet do while the counter store is unreachable — a policy question with a defensible answer in either direction, provided the reason is tied to the consequence? And what does one enormous caller do to whichever key the counters live under? The weak answer names an algorithm and stops. The strong answer names the algorithm in a sentence and spends the remaining time on where the state lives and what happens when it is gone.

**Typical realisations.** Per-key quotas on a paid API; per-user write limits on a social product; throttling failed logins, which is the variant where the availability-versus-protection answer flips.

sources.title: Design a rate limiter — a complete guide (System Design Handbook)
sources.evidence: A guide devoted to this single problem calls it a favourite interview question and gives the reason: it forces speed, accuracy, scale and fault tolerance to be traded against one another inside one answer. It also treats the choice of what to do when the limiter's own store is unreachable as the central failure question, which is the part this item grades hardest.

sources.title: Design a distributed rate limiter (Hello Interview)
sources.evidence: A coaching site's worked breakdown pins concrete non-functional targets onto the problem — a check costing under ten milliseconds, eventual consistency tolerated across nodes, a million requests a second — and grades expected depth by candidate seniority. Vendor material for a paid product, so an interested but unusually specific attestation.

sources.title: System design interview: design a rate limiter (Exponent)
sources.evidence: A recorded mock interview led by a serving engineering manager works this problem end to end, arguing about where the check belongs and whether one shared counter store spanning data centres is affordable. A mock is closer to the real event than a question list, though the page names no employer that asks it.

items.title: Per-key quotas for a metered geocoding API at 40 edge locations
items.statement_md:
You sell a geocoding API. Callers authenticate with an API key, and each key sits on a plan:

| plan | steady rate | burst ceiling | included per month |
|---|---|---|---|
| free | 60 req/min | 120 | 100 thousand |
| team | 600 req/min | 1,200 | 5 million |
| scale | 6,000 req/min | 12,000 | 250 million |

Requests terminate at 40 locations across three continents, each caller reaching whichever is nearest, and one customer's traffic routinely arrives at several locations at once. A cached lookup is answered in about 8 ms, and the product promises that quota enforcement adds no more than 2 ms at the 99th percentile.

Aggregate traffic runs around 180,000 requests per second and it is concentrated: the fifty busiest keys are about 70% of it.

Requests beyond the steady rate are refused with `429`. Volume beyond the monthly inclusion is **not** refused — it is billed as overage, and an overage line a customer disputes is expensive to investigate.

Design the enforcement path. Cover at least:

- where the accept-or-refuse decision is made, and how many network round trips it costs;
- how per-minute counters are shared across the 40 locations, or deliberately not shared, and how far above their steady rate a customer could get as a result;
- how monthly volume is recorded, given that it ends up on an invoice;
- what each location does during a 90-second outage of whatever holds the counters;
- what the fifty busiest keys do to your storage layout.

It also treats the choice of what to do when the limiter's own store is unreachable as the central failure question, which is the part this item grades hardest.

sources.evidence: A coaching site's worked breakdown pins concrete non-functional targets onto the problem — a check costing under ten milliseconds, eventual consistency tolerated across nodes, a million requests a second — and grades expected depth by candidate seniority. Vendor material for a paid product, so an interested but unusually specific attestation.

sources.evidence: A recorded mock interview led by a serving engineering manager works this problem end to end, arguing about where the check belongs and whether one shared counter store spanning data centres is affordable. A mock is closer to the real event than a question list, though the page names no employer that asks it.

hints: Work out the per-request budget before anything else. Eight milliseconds of service time and two milliseconds allowed for the check — what does that rule out immediately, given where the 40 locations are?
You are not obliged to keep one true counter. Ask what the limit is actually for: is a customer who slips 640 requests through a 600-per-minute cap a problem, and for whom?
Enforcement and billing are two different accuracy requirements applied to the same requests. Nothing says one counter has to serve both.

Consider handing each location a share of a key's per-minute budget, topped up centrally on a schedule. The hot path then never leaves the box, the worst-case overshoot is bounded by how many locations hold a share, and the outage answer becomes 'keep spending the last share you were given'.
follow_ups: One customer is 40% of all traffic and uses a single key. Where does that key's state live, and what breaks first?
Support wants to raise one customer's limit within a minute, with no deploy. What does that requirement add to your design?
The same mechanism is now asked to throttle failed logins on the account service. Which of your answers flips, and why?

criteria.description: Names an enforcement mechanism that admits the plan's burst ceiling above its steady rate, and applies it at the granularity the product actually sells on.

levels.0: Names no mechanism, or enforces a single flat rate per key with no notion of the burst ceiling sitting above the steady rate.
levels.2: Names a mechanism that can admit a burst — a token bucket, or a window with a separate burst allowance — but leaves the granularity vague, or never connects it to the two numbers each plan carries.
levels.4: Names the mechanism in a sentence and pins it to this product: a bucket per key refilling at that plan's steady rate with its depth set by the burst ceiling, saying which plan number each parameter comes from, and does not spend the rest of the answer on the algorithm.

criteria.description: Places the accept-or-refuse decision somewhere that can meet the stated 2 ms p99 and counts the round trips it costs, rather than treating a counter lookup as free.

levels.0: Routes every request to one central store with no mention of the distance to it, or offers no latency reasoning anywhere.
levels.2: Recognises that a cross-continent hop is too slow and keeps state near the request, but never compares the resulting cost against the 2 ms figure.
levels.4: Says where the decision is made, counts the hops on the hot path and argues the total against the 2 ms budget, and states what happens on a local miss or a cold process.

criteria.description: Explains how counters are reconciled across the 40 locations and quantifies the resulting overshoot, instead of asserting the limit holds exactly.

levels.0: Claims exact fleet-wide enforcement with no mechanism behind it, or ignores that one key is seen at several locations at once.
levels.2: Proposes local counters with periodic synchronisation but cannot say how far past the limit a customer gets before a sync catches it.
levels.4: Names the scheme — budget shares allocated per location, or local counting on a stated sync interval — derives the worst-case overshoot from it in requests, and argues why that error is acceptable for a rate cap.

criteria.description: Keeps the approximate enforcement counter apart from the durable record the invoice is built from, and says how the durable one is written and checked.

levels.0: Invoices straight from the in-memory enforcement counters, or never says how monthly volume is captured at all.
levels.2: Emits usage records to a durable pipeline but treats the invoice as whatever that pipeline happens to total, with no reconciliation and no dispute path.
levels.4: Keeps enforcement approximate and billing durable, describes how usage records get from an edge location to the billing store, and names the check that would catch a location dropping records before a customer notices.

criteria.description: Names an allow-through or refuse-all policy for the 90-second counter-store outage, ties the reason to this product's consequences, and says what each location runs on meanwhile.

levels.0: Never considers the store being unreachable, or waves it away as highly available and moves on.
levels.2: Names the choice between allowing and refusing traffic during the outage but picks one without connecting it to this API's risk, and says nothing about the counters afterwards.
levels.4: Picks a policy justified by the actual consequence — an unmetered free tier versus paying customers refused service — falls back to the last known share or a conservative local cap for the duration, and says how counters and usage records settle up once the store returns.

items.title: Price alerts for a watchlist service at the opening bell
items.statement_md:
A brokerage lets customers put instruments on a watchlist and set a price alert on any of
them. When a price crosses a customer's threshold they get a push notification.

The shape of the data:

| | |
|---|---|
| instruments quoted | 9,000 |
| customers | 6 million |
| watchlist entries | 140 million, so about 23 per customer |
| the most-watched instrument | on 4.1 million watchlists |
| the median instrument | on 900 watchlists |

Prices arrive as a stream of ticks, roughly 30,000 a second through the session. In the
first ninety seconds after the open that rises to about 400,000 a second, and the crossings
cluster: a single instrument moving through a round number can put several hundred thousand
customers over their threshold within a second or two.

Customers also open the app. A watchlist view is one screen showing all 23 of their
instruments with current prices, and it is read far more often than any alert fires.

An alert that arrives four minutes late is worthless — the price has moved. A duplicate is
worse than late.

Design the alerting path. Cover at least:

- how a tick becomes the set of customers to notify, and how many of those evaluations
  happen per second at the open;
- where the fanout for the most-watched instrument happens, and what you do differently for
  it than for the median one;
- what the watchlist screen reads, and whether it shares anything with the alert path;
- what the whole thing does when notification delivery backs up for two minutes.

hints: Start with the number the design has to survive. At the open, how many customer-threshold comparisons does one second of ticks imply if you do the obvious thing?
The most-watched instrument and the median one are four thousand times apart. Is one mechanism going to be right for both?
A threshold is a number per customer per instrument. What structure lets one tick find the customers who just crossed without touching the ones who did not?
The watchlist screen is 23 reads of the same prices everyone else is reading. What does that let you cache that the alert path cannot?
follow_ups: A customer sets an alert on the most-watched instrument at a price it is currently sitting on. What happens, and how do you avoid notifying them once a second?
The product wants alerts on a two-instrument condition — one above, one below. What breaks?
How would you tell, in production, that a customer's alert did not fire when it should have?

criteria.description: Turns the tick rate and the watchlist skew into the number of threshold evaluations per second, and names the worst single instrument rather than reasoning about an average one.

levels.0: No arithmetic at all, or a single average-case number that never mentions the 4.1-million-watchlist instrument.
levels.2: Computes a rate from ticks times average watchers, but treats the most-watched instrument as a larger version of the same case rather than a different one.
levels.4: Derives the evaluation rate at the open, computes what one tick on the most-watched instrument costs on its own, and uses the gap between that and the median to justify the design that follows.

criteria.description: Decides where the fan-out from one tick to many customers happens, and treats the head of the distribution differently from the tail rather than picking one mechanism for both.

levels.0: One mechanism for every instrument, with no acknowledgement that the top one is thousands of times wider than the median.
levels.2: Splits head from tail, but the boundary is asserted with no reasoning about where it should sit, or the head's path is described without saying what makes it cheaper.
levels.4: Head and tail handled by different mechanisms, with the boundary derived from the numbers given, the cost of each path stated, and the reason the head's mechanism would be wrong for the tail made explicit.

criteria.description: Describes a structure that finds the customers a tick just moved past without scanning the ones it did not, and says how that structure is partitioned and kept current.

levels.0: Scans every watcher of the instrument on every tick, or leaves the lookup unspecified.
levels.2: Names an ordered structure per instrument so only crossings are touched, but says nothing about how it is partitioned or what updating it costs when a customer edits an alert.
levels.4: Names the structure, says what it is keyed and ordered by, partitions it in a way that keeps one instrument's traffic from one place, and states the cost of an alert being added or moved.

criteria.description: Says what the watchlist screen reads and whether it shares state with the alert path, and what the system does when notification delivery falls behind.

levels.0: Never distinguishes the read path from the alert path, or assumes delivery never backs up.
levels.2: Caches prices for the screen and notes that delivery could back up, but does not say what is dropped or delayed when it does, given that a late alert is worthless.
levels.4: States what the screen reads and how stale it may be, and gives a policy for a delivery backlog that follows from 'four minutes late is worthless' — shedding rather than queueing, and what the customer sees as a result.

sources.evidence: An interview-prep site publishes a full worked answer for a service that receives third-party callbacks, and puts at-least-once processing in its non-functional requirements rather than in a footnote. Its expected mechanism is a stored event identifier checked before the effect runs, which shows the question is about duplicates and retries, not the happy path.

sources.evidence: A system-design interview guide keeps a standalone entry pairing repeat-safe effects with event sequencing, and frames both as things a candidate is expected to demonstrate. It names no employers and offers no sample prompts, so treat it as a weak attestation whose value is being a second, unrelated publisher covering the same pairing.

sources.evidence: An interview curriculum marks its asynchronous-delivery problem high priority and builds the expected answer on queues, exponential backoff and a dead-letter path, with the choice between at-least-once and exactly-once presented as something the candidate must resolve aloud. Corroborates the same line of questioning from a different problem statement.

hints: The scanner retries until it gets a 2xx. What does that guarantee, and what does it emphatically not guarantee?
Exactly-once processing is not on offer from a sender that retries. An effect that can run twice and leave the same count is — what would you key that on?
Check-then-decrement is a race the moment two deliveries of the same scan arrive together. What makes it one step instead of two?
The backlog is the interesting case: it is a burst from one device, all of it old. Does it need to be fast, and what should the service answer if it cannot take it now?
follow_ups: A picker scans an item, then puts it back and scans a `return`. Does that change how you key duplicates?
Two scanners pick the last unit of the same item within a second of each other. What does the count do, and what should the second picker see?
The device clock is wrong by three hours. Does anything in your design depend on it?

criteria.description: Names the exact field duplicates are collapsed on and puts the duplicate record and the count change in one atomic commit, rather than checking and then writing.

levels.0: Keys on something that changes between attempts — arrival time, a hash including headers — or does not deduplicate at all.
levels.2: Keys on the scan identifier, but the check and the decrement are separate steps and nothing is said about two deliveries arriving at once.
levels.4: Keys on the scan identifier, commits the duplicate record and the decrement together or lets a unique constraint reject the second writer, and says what the loser of that race returns to the device.

criteria.description: States what must be durable before the service answers 2xx, and what it answers when it cannot accept the scan, given that the device will retry either way.

levels.0: Answers 2xx before anything is durable without saying what a crash loses, or never says what a refusal looks like.
levels.2: Names what is durable before the acknowledgement, but treats a lost acknowledgement as impossible or gives no retryable failure response.
levels.4: States exactly what is durable before 2xx, returns a status that keeps the device retrying under pressure rather than one that makes it give up, and says what a lost acknowledgement costs — nothing, because the redelivery is a duplicate.

criteria.description: Handles a reconnecting scanner dumping hours of old scans at once, without letting it displace live traffic or lose the backlog.

levels.0: Treats the backlog as ordinary traffic, or drops it, or assumes the service simply absorbs it.
levels.2: Notices the burst and buffers it, but says nothing about what happens when the buffer fills or about the backlog competing with live scans.
levels.4: Separates or paces the backlog so a live scan is not stuck behind two hours of old ones, bounds what is accepted at once, and says why the old scans can afford to be slow while the live ones cannot.

criteria.description: Names how a divergence between the counted stock and the physical shelf would be discovered, rather than assuming the ledger is the truth.

levels.0: Treats the stored count as correct by construction, or offers no way to find out it is wrong.
levels.2: Mentions cycle counts or an audit but gives no signal, cadence or threshold, and no account of what is done with a discrepancy.
levels.4: Gives a concrete detection route — a periodic physical count on the fastest-moving items, or an alert on a pick against a zero count — with a cadence tied to how quickly a wrong count causes a stalled order, and says what correcting it does to the event history.

items.title: Throttling failed sign-ins for a consumer app
items.statement_md:
A consumer app has 30 million accounts and takes sign-ins at 12 points of presence. Steady
traffic is about 3,000 sign-in attempts a second, and roughly 6% of them fail.

You need to throttle failed attempts so that guessing a password is not practical, without
locking real people out of their own accounts.

What is known about the traffic:

- credential-stuffing runs arrive in bursts: one campaign was 40,000 attempts a minute
  against 12,000 distinct accounts, from 9,000 distinct addresses, spread across all 12
  points of presence;
- a real person who has forgotten their password typically gets it wrong three or four times
  in a couple of minutes, from one address;
- a shared office or a mobile carrier puts thousands of unrelated people behind one address.

The sign-in path has an 80 ms budget at the 99th percentile, and the throttle check sits
inside it.

Design the throttle. Cover at least:

- what the limit is counted against, and why that choice does not lock out a carrier's whole
  customer base;
- where the accept-or-refuse decision is made, and how many network round trips it costs;
- how the counters are shared across the 12 points of presence, or deliberately not, and how
  far a determined attacker gets as a result;
- what each point of presence does during a 90-second outage of whatever holds the counters.

sources.title: Design a rate limiter — a complete guide (System Design Handbook)
sources.evidence: A guide devoted to this single problem calls it a favourite interview question and gives the reason: it forces speed, accuracy, scale and fault tolerance to be traded against one another inside one answer. It also treats the choice of what to do when the limiter's own store is unreachable as the central failure question, which is the part this item grades hardest.

sources.title: Design a distributed rate limiter (Hello Interview)
sources.evidence: A coaching site's worked breakdown pins concrete non-functional targets onto the problem — a check costing under ten milliseconds, eventual consistency tolerated across nodes, a million requests a second — and grades expected depth by candidate seniority. Vendor material for a paid product, so an interested but unusually specific attestation.

sources.title: System design interview: design a rate limiter (Exponent)
sources.evidence: A recorded mock interview led by a serving engineering manager works this problem end to end, arguing about where the check belongs and whether one shared counter store spanning data centres is affordable. A mock is closer to the real event than a question list, though the page names no employer that asks it.

hints: What is the thing you are actually protecting — an account, or the service? The answer decides what the counter is keyed on.
Counting per address punishes a carrier's whole customer base; counting per account lets an attacker spread across accounts freely. Does it have to be one or the other?
The 80 ms budget includes this check. Where does the counter have to live for that to hold at twelve locations?

Now the counter store is gone for 90 seconds. This is a sign-in path — is allowing everything through or refusing everything the safer failure here, and is that the same answer you would give for a metered API?
follow_ups: The attacker switches to one attempt per account per hour across two million accounts. Does your throttle see it?
A real customer is locked out at the airport on the morning of a flight. What does your design give them?
How would you tell a credential-stuffing campaign from a broken client retrying in a loop?

criteria.description: Chooses what the counter is keyed on and defends it against both failure modes named in the brief — a shared address punishing innocents, and an attacker spreading thinly across accounts.

levels.0: One limit per address, or one per account, with no acknowledgement of what that choice gives away.
levels.2: Uses more than one key, but does not say what each is for, or picks per-account only and never addresses an attacker who spreads across many accounts.
levels.4: Names each key and the attack or accident it exists for — per account against guessing one password, per address against a single source, and something broader against a distributed campaign — with thresholds tied to the traffic given rather than round numbers.

criteria.description: Places the accept-or-refuse decision where the 80 ms budget can hold across twelve locations, and counts what it costs rather than treating a counter lookup as free.

levels.0: Sends every attempt to one central store with no mention of the distance to it, or offers no latency reasoning at all.
levels.2: Keeps state near the request because a cross-region hop is slow, but never compares the resulting cost against the 80 ms figure.
levels.4: Says where the decision is made, counts the hops on the hot path, argues the total against the budget, and says what happens on a local miss or a cold process.

criteria.description: Explains how counters are reconciled across the twelve points of presence and quantifies how many extra attempts an attacker gets, instead of asserting the limit holds exactly.

levels.0: Claims exact fleet-wide enforcement with no mechanism, or ignores that one campaign hits all twelve locations at once.
levels.2: Proposes local counters with periodic synchronisation but cannot say how many attempts slip through before a sync catches up.
levels.4: Names the scheme, derives the worst-case overshoot in attempts from the sync interval and the number of locations, and argues whether that number is acceptable for guessing a password specifically.

criteria.description: Picks an allow-through or refuse-all policy for the 90-second counter outage and ties it to this product's consequence, which is not the same consequence a metered API has.

levels.0: Never considers the store being unreachable, or waves it away as highly available.
levels.2: Names the choice between allowing and refusing but picks one without connecting it to what an unthrottled sign-in path costs.
levels.4: Picks a policy justified by the actual consequence — ninety unthrottled seconds is a free guessing window, which is a different trade from an unmetered API's — falls back to a conservative local cap for the duration, and says how counters settle up afterwards.

items.title: Distribute traffic across a pool whose membership keeps changing
items.statement_md:
**Pattern.** One entry point stands in front of a pool of backends, and the interviewer keeps changing the pool underneath it: an instance degrades rather than dies, a deploy cycles every member, a dependency they all share has a bad minute, capacity is added and removed mid-answer. The candidate has to say which backend an arriving request goes to, and defend that rule while the pool moves.

**What it measures.** Whether the distribution rule is derived from the shape of the work instead of picked off a list — handing requests out in turn equalises arrivals, which stops being the same thing as equalising load once service times spread over two orders of magnitude, and every work-aware rule has one failure it actively makes worse, since an instance that fails instantly looks like the idlest member of the pool. Whether the health probe is treated as a signal that can be wrong in two directions: too shallow and a broken process keeps being fed, too deep and one shared dependency fails every member at once and empties the pool. Whether taking a backend away is a period rather than an event — what becomes of work already in flight, and of whatever a client was relying on staying put. And whether affinity is argued from what a backend actually holds, rather than reached for by default or refused by reflex.

**Typical realisations.** An HTTP tier serving request-scoped work; a fleet terminating connections that live for hours; a tier where a request has exactly one correct destination and evenness is a constraint rather than the goal.

sources.title: Load balancer — system design interview question (GeeksforGeeks)
sources.evidence: A 37-question guide devoted to this one component, framed explicitly as interview preparation: it works through choosing among round robin, weighted variants, source-IP hash, least connections and least response time by workload, then through active versus passive probing, session persistence and failover. Aggregator material rather than a first-hand account, but unambiguous that the topic stands on its own rather than appearing only as a box inside a larger design.

sources.title: Design a load balancer (AlgoMaster)
sources.evidence: A worked breakdown that ranks designing the balancer itself as a high-priority interview topic and builds the answer up in stages the way the event runs. Health checking is stated as a functional requirement rather than an aside; the page argues for a weighted work-aware rule when backends differ and request cost varies, and covers letting existing connections finish when a backend is withdrawn.

sources.title: Load balancing in system design: algorithms and interview use cases (Crack The Offer)
sources.evidence: Presents the topic as senior-level reasoning and — the part that matters for grading — contrasts a weak answer that reaches for the simplest rotation with a strong one that ties the choice to traffic shape, separates short uniform calls from long-lived sockets, and folds probing and the loss of an availability zone into the same answer.

sources.title: What interviewers actually want to hear about load balancing (mayhemcode)
sources.evidence: A prep post whose claim is that the probe's depth is what gets pushed on, not its existence — an endpoint that answers 200 while the process cannot reach its database is the trap it names — and that affinity should be argued from what the process keeps in memory. Written as predicted expectations rather than from transcripts, so it corroborates the emphasis without independently proving the question is put.

hints: Read the cost table before choosing anything. A rule that hands renders out in turn equalises one quantity — is it the quantity that runs out on a worker?

There are two questions hiding inside "is this worker healthy": is this process broken, and is the world broken. What should the entry point do when the answer to the second is yes for all 120 at once?
Take whatever rule you picked and walk one specific worker through it — the one whose renderer is dead and which answers in three milliseconds. Where does it rank?

Consider: rank workers by renders currently outstanding against their 8 slots rather than in turn; keep the shared object store out of the pass-or-fail decision and add a floor below which the entry point stops believing the probes at all; eject on error rates seen in real responses, not only on probe results; and stop assigning new work before a worker is removed, with the wait set from the render tail rather than a round number.
follow_ups: One customer starts submitting 300-page reports at 50 a second on a single key. What does your rule do, and what do the other customers see?
The entry point is one box on your diagram. How many of them are actually running, and how do they agree about which workers are healthy?
Renders move behind a queue instead — clients submit and poll for the result. Which parts of your answer survive, and which stop being distribution problems at all?

criteria.description: Picks the rule that assigns an arriving render to a worker and derives it from the cost distribution and the 8-slot concurrency, rather than naming an algorithm from a list.

levels.0: Hands renders out in turn because it is simple and even, or defers a work-aware rule to later if imbalance shows up without saying what would show it, or says the load balancer will take care of it — in every case with no reference to a mean that is thirteen times the median and no mention of the two hardware generations.
levels.2: Names a work-aware rule such as fewest connections and says it copes better with uneven requests, but never ties it to the numbers given, does not say what the entry point must track to run it, and leaves the slower generation to a weight someone sets by hand.
levels.4: Argues that evening out arrivals is not evening out work at this spread, so ranks workers by renders outstanding against their 8 slots (or by shortest expected queue), notes that the same rule absorbs the 40% slower generation with no weight to tune, and names the price — the entry point now carries per-worker state, which rules out a stateless DNS or connection-level spray.

criteria.description: Says what the probe actually tests and what the entry point does when the shared object store degrades and the whole pool starts failing that probe simultaneously.

levels.0: Adds a health endpoint without saying what it tests, or proposes a deep probe that exercises the object store and the licence service on every check — and either way treats a failed check as proof that the worker should leave the pool.
levels.2: Splits a shallow liveness probe from a deeper readiness probe, or sets reasonable intervals and consecutive-failure thresholds, but still lets the pool empty in the case where the shared dependency is the thing that is broken.
levels.4: Scopes the probe to what is genuinely local to a worker — the renderer subprocess, its own queue depth — keeps the shared object store out of the pass-or-fail decision, and gives the entry point a floor: below some healthy fraction it stops trusting the probes and spreads across everyone, on the argument that a degraded worker beats no worker. States the interval and the failure count and what those cost in probe traffic against 120 workers.

criteria.description: Works out what the chosen rule does with the worker that returns a 500 in 3 ms, and reacts to it on observed traffic rather than only on a probe.

levels.0: Does not consider it, or asserts the health probe will catch it without saying how much traffic the worker takes in the meantime.
levels.2: Sees that the broken worker has to be ejected and leaves that to the periodic probe, without noticing that a rule based on outstanding work ranks an instantly-failing worker as the least busy member of the pool.
levels.4: States the interaction plainly: a worker that answers in 3 ms is never busy, so a work-aware rule steers a growing share of traffic into it and the failure amplifies itself — then answers with a signal taken from real responses, such as error-rate or latency outlier ejection, gives a re-admission rule that does not flap, and estimates what share of renders the worker swallows before it goes.

criteria.description: Says what happens to renders already running on a worker that a rolling deploy or a scale-in is about to remove, and bounds the wait with a number taken from the render tail.

levels.0: Removes the worker and lets whatever it was rendering fail, never mentions in-flight work at all, or claims that turning connection draining on makes the deploy zero-downtime without once comparing the drain window against a 90-second render.
levels.2: Says the worker is drained before it goes, but chooses no window, or chooses one without reference to the 90-second timeout and the 11-second 99th percentile the wait has to outlast.
levels.4: Stops new assignments first and lets running renders finish, sets the window from the tail rather than a round number, says what happens to a render still going when the window expires — killed and resubmitted elsewhere, against the client's own timeout — and notes that draining 120 workers inside 20 minutes overlaps, so usable capacity dips while the deploy runs.

criteria.description: Decides whether a customer's renders should keep landing on the same worker, and argues it from what a worker actually keeps between requests.

levels.0: Pins each customer to a worker so their template cache stays warm, without asking what a worker holds between renders or what pinning costs when the pool changes every five minutes.
levels.2: Rules stickiness out because stateless is better, or rules it in because caching is good, without naming the state a render actually needs or what the pool's churn does to any pinning.
levels.4: Names what a worker holds — a font and template cache that is a hit-rate optimisation and not correctness — and concludes that renders stay interchangeable, so no affinity is taken and the pool may change freely. If affinity is argued for anyway, it is a preference that may be dropped the moment balance demands it, and the candidate says what becomes of it across a deploy that replaces all 120 workers.

items.title: Placing live editing sessions across a 400-node collaboration tier

sources.title: Load balancer — system design interview question (GeeksforGeeks)
sources.evidence: A 37-question guide devoted to this one component, framed explicitly as interview preparation: it works through choosing among round robin, weighted variants, source-IP hash, least connections and least response time by workload, then through active versus passive probing, session persistence and failover. hints: Before choosing an algorithm, decide whether the entry point has a choice at all. If a document lives in exactly one place, what is left for a distribution rule to decide?
Add one backend. Write down what changed about the mapping, and then write down what that change does to sockets that were already open.
A single healthy-or-not verdict has to answer two different questions here: may this backend take a new document, and should the 4,000 people already on it be thrown off. Are those the same question?

Sketch one step of the rolling deploy minute by minute: a backend goes, 4,000 clients see their socket close, they reconnect. Where do they land, how fast do they arrive, and what does the receiving backend see? Then say what you would change on the client so that step is survivable 400 times in a row.
follow_ups: A backend is reclaimed with no warning. How long until its 1,700 documents are editable again, and which component owns that number?
Product wants a document to stay editable offline and sync when the client comes back. Does that change where the document has to live?
You are asked to run this tier in two regions. What is the first thing about your mapping that stops working?

criteria.description: Explains how a connection reaches the backend that owns its document, and why a rule that chases the least busy backend is the wrong instrument here.

levels.0: Spreads new connections over the 400 backends by rotation or by fewest connections, terminates them anywhere and reads the document from storage on each edit, or asserts a least-busy rule and a per-document shard in the same answer without noticing they name different destinations — single ownership is dropped without it being noticed.
levels.2: Routes by hashing the document identifier so the owner is found, but presents that as a way of spreading load, and never separates where a document lives from how busy the backend holding it is.
levels.4: Holds the two questions apart: the destination follows ownership — a hash or a directory every entry point agrees on — and evenness is bought somewhere else, in how ownership is assigned rather than in where a socket is sent. Says what the entry point must know to route a connection and what that lookup costs on connect, and notes that once a socket is open no rebalancing may move it without breaking it.

criteria.description: Quantifies what going from 400 backends to 401 does to the document mapping, and connects a remapped document to the live connections it costs.

levels.0: Maps documents with a hash taken modulo the backend count, claims both that mapping and consistent hashing without noticing they are different mappings, or does not say what happens when a backend is added or lost.
levels.2: Names a hash ring or consistent hashing and says most keys stay put, but gives no figure for how much moves at 400 to 401, and never says that a moved document means live sockets closed.
levels.4: Gives the fraction — about one four-hundredth of open documents, on the order of 1,700 of the 700 thousand, roughly one backend's worth — says those editors are disconnected and their in-memory state is rebuilt from storage on the new owner, and contrasts it with a modulo mapping, where nearly every document changes hands and the whole tier reconnects at once.

criteria.description: Handles the published document with 30 thousand viewers on a backend sized for 4,000 connections, without abandoning single ownership of the edit path.

levels.0: Assumes hashing spreads the load evenly, or moves the popular document to a larger backend and treats that as the answer.
levels.2: Notices the owning backend will be swamped and reaches for replication or caching, but does not separate the editors, who must reach the owner, from the read-only viewers, who need not.
levels.4: Splits the two populations: edits still go to the single owner, while viewers are served by a relay tier that subscribes to the owner once and re-broadcasts, so the owner's connection count is bounded by editors rather than by audience. Says how a viewer who starts editing is promoted, and what signal tells the system a document has gone hot in the first place.

criteria.description: Says what a failed probe should mean for a backend holding 4,000 live connections, and what the tier does with one that can serve what it has but should take nothing new.

levels.0: Applies the policy an HTTP pool uses — two failed probes and the backend leaves rotation — with no acknowledgement that removing it disconnects four thousand people.
levels.2: Notes the stakes are higher and stretches the interval or the failure count, but keeps one healthy-or-unhealthy verdict, so a backend that should merely stop taking new documents can only be removed outright.
levels.4: Separates may-take-new-sessions from is-still-serving-the-ones-it-has and drives them from different signals, argues the ejection threshold from what an ejection costs — a false positive here is a mass disconnection, so it is slower and more hysteretic than an HTTP pool's — and says what a genuinely dead backend's 1,700 documents do: who notices, who takes ownership, and how the editors find the new owner.

criteria.description: Works out what a rolling deploy does to connections that outlive it, and what the tier sees in the seconds after a backend's clients reconnect.

levels.0: Says connections are drained gracefully before each backend is replaced, without noticing that the 95th percentile session runs past six hours and a deploy cannot wait it out — or leaves the return traffic to the clients' own backoff without ever asking what rate they come back at.
levels.2: Accepts that connections have to be broken and mentions reconnect backoff, but does not say where the 4,000 clients land, or assumes their return is spread out simply because clients retry.
levels.4: Treats the disconnection as deliberate and shaped: the server closes with a reason and a randomised delay rather than letting every socket race back, the candidate compares the resulting arrival rate against the tier's steady connect rate, and observes that reconnects re-derive the same owner, so the surge lands on whichever backends the mapping names rather than on the pool as a whole. Says what paces the deploy so 400 steps do not add up to a rolling brownout.
